lesson.title: Set Math: Intersection, Difference, and Symmetric Difference
lesson.summary: Python sets support the core operations of mathematical set theory directly, letting you find shared elements, unique elements, and elements that belong to exactly one set with a single operator or method call.
lesson.body:
One of the biggest reasons Sets exist as their own data type, rather than just being lists with duplicates removed, is that Python lets you combine sets the way you would combine sets in math class, using operators borrowed straight from set theory. Given two sets, you can ask what they share, what one has that the other does not, and what belongs to exactly one of them but not both.

morning_class = {"Ana", "Ben", "Cleo", "Dev"}
afternoon_class = {"Cleo", "Dev", "Eli"}

print(sorted(morning_class & afternoon_class))
print(sorted(morning_class - afternoon_class))
print(sorted(morning_class ^ afternoon_class))

The & operator is intersection, and it prints ['Cleo', 'Dev'], the students enrolled in both classes. The - operator is difference, and morning_class - afternoon_class prints ['Ana', 'Ben'], the students in the morning class who are not also in the afternoon class; notice this is not symmetric, since afternoon_class - morning_class would give a different answer. The ^ operator is symmetric difference, and it prints ['Ana', 'Ben', 'Eli'], every student who appears in exactly one of the two classes but not both. Each operator also has a matching method, intersection(), difference(), and symmetric_difference(), which do the same thing and read a little more clearly in longer expressions.

Sets also support methods that change a set in place, unlike the read-only operators above. add() inserts a single new element, and there are two ways to remove one: discard(), which does nothing if the value is not present, and remove(), which raises an error if it is not.

pantry = {"flour", "sugar"}
pantry.add("eggs")
pantry.discard("salt")
print(sorted(pantry))

try:
    pantry.remove("salt")
except KeyError as e:
    print("Error:", e)

The first print shows ['eggs', 'flour', 'sugar']: add("eggs") worked as expected, and discard("salt") quietly did nothing since "salt" was never in the pantry to begin with. The second block prints Error: 'salt', because remove(), unlike discard(), insists the element actually be present and raises a KeyError naming the missing value when it is not. One more operation you will meet again soon in its own dedicated lesson is union, which combines two sets together rather than comparing them; it deserves the closer look that Set Union gives it next.
